name: Oral antibiotics (doxycycline/minocycline)
lead: Doxycycline and minocycline are tetracycline-class antibiotics that dermatologists prescribe for inflammatory acne and rosacea. Both are prescription-only in the US and other countries [1][2].

Wikipedia reports that doxycycline is used at higher doses for severe acne and rosacea and at lower subantimicrobial doses long term, with benefit thought to come partly from anti-inflammatory effects [1]. Minocycline is approved for inflammatory lesions of moderate-to-severe acne in people aged nine and older, with oral courses typically three to four months and limited data beyond that [2]. Because of antibiotic resistance, oral antibiotics are generally combined with topical acne treatments [2].

paras: Both drugs treat a range of infections. For acne and rosacea, doxycycline is used at antimicrobial or subantimicrobial doses [1]. Minocycline is used for inflammatory acne, though Wikipedia says it is generally less preferred than doxycycline for other infections [2].
Doxycycline: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, increased sunburn risk, and pill esophagitis if taken without enough fluid. It is FDA pregnancy category D [1].

Minocycline: long-term use can cause blue-gray pigmentation of skin, nails and scars; drug-induced lupus and autoimmune hepatitis, more often in women; vestibular effects such as dizziness and tinnitus; and rarely intracranial hypertension [2]. The US label warns that tetracycline-class drugs can cause fetal harm and permanent tooth discoloration if used during tooth development [3].

Both are mainly bacteriostatic, binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis [1][2][3]. Doxycycline also reduces neutrophil chemotaxis and inhibits matrix metalloproteinases [1].

Registered trials include a 528-person phase 3 trial of 40 mg doxycycline versus placebo in rosacea [4], a comparison of spironolactone versus doxycycline for acne (n=350) [5], and a trial of metformin versus doxycycline in adult acne [6]. A study of subantimicrobial doxycycline in acne has also been registered [7]. Results are not summarised here. Preclinical studies of minocycline in stroke and neurodegeneration models are not related to appearance use.
Doxycycline was developed at Pfizer, patented in 1957 and FDA-approved in 1967 [1]. Minocycline was patented in 1961 and sold from 1971; a topical acne foam was approved in 2019 [2].

On looksmax.org, one user described taking a high amount of minocycline with persistent acne and asked about adding a second antibiotic. Replies said diet matters, that antibiotics disrupt gut flora, and suggested retinoid-based topicals instead [8].

timeline.event: Topical minocycline foam approved for acne [2].

claims.claim: Antibiotics destroy gut flora and should be avoided unless truly needed
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply said antibiotics damage gut flora and recommended retinoid products instead [8].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that resistance is a growing concern leading clinicians to combine oral antibiotics with topicals [2]. Studies of gut effects of acne antibiotics were not found in the sources consulted.

card.summary: Prescription tetracyclines for inflammatory acne; established in dermatology, with documented side effects and resistance concerns.
card.note: Pregnancy and tooth-development warnings; minocycline pigmentation and lupus-like reactions.

quick.overview:
Doxycycline and minocycline are oral antibiotics that dermatologists prescribe for inflammatory acne and rosacea. They are usually paired with topical treatments.

Forum users discuss them for stubborn acne, with some voicing gut-health concerns.
quick.mechanism: They inhibit bacterial protein synthesis and also have anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.risks: Doxycycline: GI upset, sun sensitivity, esophagitis. Minocycline: pigmentation, drug-induced lupus, dizziness, rare intracranial hypertension. Both are warned against in pregnancy and childhood tooth development. Prescription-only.
